# Welcome {#welcome .unnumbered}

::: {.tada-hero}
<p class="tada-eyebrow">Best practice for code sharing</p>

## Code that still runs when someone else opens it {.unlisted .unnumbered}

Most of the analytical code behind published papers is never shared, and a good
deal of what is shared does not run. This wiki covers four things you can do to
a project before you submit it that, between them, fix most of the problem.
:::

## What this wiki is {.unnumbered}

Sharing code is essential for transparency and computational reproducibility,
and journal policies increasingly require it. Even so, the proportion of papers
in ecology and evolutionary biology that share code remains low, with reported
rates ranging from roughly **5% to 33%**, well behind the equivalent figures for
open data. Code that is shared also frequently fails to run. In a review of over
9,000 R files archived in the Harvard Dataverse, **74% failed to complete
without error**, and that figure only fell to **56%** after automated cleaning
(removing local file paths and fixing library installation and loading). A study
of species distribution and abundance papers abandoned its reproducibility
assessment altogether because **93% of scripts** either did not run or ran with
errors.

One reason is that researchers are rarely taught how to archive analytical code.
The resources that do exist are written largely for *software developers*, not
for someone preparing a one-off analysis of a single dataset.

**TADA** (Transferable, Available, Documented, Annotated) is a set of simple
guidelines aimed at that gap. This wiki expands them into a working reference and
sets them alongside the practices that go with them: metadata, licences,
repository choice, the SORTEE data and code quality control guidelines, and code
review.

## The four principles {.unnumbered}

::: {.tada-cards}
::: {.tada-card .t}
[T]{.tada-letter} [Transferable]{.tada-word}
[Anyone can open your file and run it on their own machine, without converting
or editing it first.]{.tada-gloss}
:::

::: {.tada-card .a1}
[A]{.tada-letter} [Available]{.tada-word}
[The code is publicly archived somewhere immutable, with a persistent
identifier (a DOI) that is cited in the paper.]{.tada-gloss}
:::

::: {.tada-card .d}
[D]{.tada-letter} [Documented]{.tada-word}
[A README describes the files, the software environment, the licence, and
where the data live.]{.tada-gloss}
:::

::: {.tada-card .a2}
[A]{.tada-letter} [Annotated]{.tada-word}
[Comments inside the code say what each chunk does, why it is needed and which
result in the paper it produces.]{.tada-gloss}
:::
:::

::: {.tada-key}
TADA is deliberately a **minimum standard**. Analytical code is usually written
for one dataset and one study, and its job is to be a transparent, reproducible
record of that analysis rather than reusable software. TADA sets the bar at what
that job requires, and maps onto the FAIR principles as it does so.
:::

## How to use this wiki {.unnumbered}

| If you want to… | Go to |
|---|---|
| Get code ready to submit | [Start here](#quickstart) |
| Understand TADA and how it maps to FAIR | [TADA at a glance](#tada) |
| Work through one principle at a time | [Transferable](#transferable), [Available](#available), [Documented](#documented), [Annotated](#annotated) |
| Write a README, pick a licence, choose a repository | [Data & code sharing](#data-sharing) |
| Know what a journal data editor will check | [The SORTEE guidelines](#sortee) |
| Set up or run a code review | [Code review](#code-review) |
| Find guides, tutorials and papers | [Further reading](#further-reading) |
| Add a page to this wiki | [Contribute](#contribute) |

Each chapter stands on its own, so you can arrive from a search and read only
the section you need. Cross-references will take you to the rest.

## Who this is for {.unnumbered}

Researchers at any level of coding experience who need to share the code behind
a paper. The examples use R and Python, since those are the languages most used
in ecology and evolutionary biology, but the principles apply equally to
workflow languages such as Snakemake, to compiled languages such as C++, and to
disciplines well beyond ecology.

You do not need to know Git, Docker or unit testing to follow this wiki. Where
those tools are useful they are mentioned, but always as optional extras rather
than requirements.

## Where the guidance comes from {.unnumbered}

This wiki draws on three sources, all of which are worth reading in full. Copies,
and their terms of use, are in [`papers/`](papers/README.md).

- **Ivimey-Cook, E. R., Culina, A., Dimri, S., Grainger, M. J., Kar, F.,
  Lagisz, M., Moran, N. P., Nakagawa, S., Roche, D. G., Tattan, S.,
  Sánchez-Tójar, A., Windecker, S. M., & Pick, J. L.** *TADA! Simple guidelines
  to improve analytical code sharing for transparency and reproducibility.*
  <br>*Underpins* the four TADA principles and the
  [Transferable](#transferable), [Available](#available),
  [Documented](#documented) and [Annotated](#annotated) chapters.

- **Pick, J. L., Allen, B. J., Bachelot, B., Bairos-Novak, K. R., Brand, J. A.,
  Class, B., Dallas, T., D'Amelio, P. B., Fenollosa, E., Fernández-Juricic, E.,
  Gomes, D. G. E., Grainger, M. J., Guillemaud, T., John, C., Krasnow, R.,
  Lagisz, M., Lequime, S., Maynard, D. S., Nakagawa, S., O'Dea, R. E.,
  Paquet, M., Petitjean, Q., Sánchez-Tójar, A., van Dis, N. E., Wilson, L. A. B.,
  & Ivimey-Cook, E. R. (2026).** *The SORTEE guidelines for data and code
  quality control in ecology and evolutionary biology.* **Peer Community
  Journal 6: e20.** <https://doi.org/10.24072/pcjournal.687>
  <br>*Underpins* the [SORTEE guidelines](#sortee) section and most of
  [Data & code sharing](#data-sharing).

- **Ivimey-Cook, E. R., Pick, J. L., Bairos-Novak, K. R., Culina, A.,
  Gould, E., Grainger, M., Marshall, B. M., Moreau, D., Paquet, M.,
  Royauté, R., Sánchez-Tójar, A., Silva, I., & Windecker, S. M. (2023).**
  *Implementing code review in the scientific workflow: Insights from ecology
  and evolutionary biology.* **Journal of Evolutionary Biology 36: 1347–1356.**
  <https://doi.org/10.1111/jeb.14230>
  <br>*Underpins* the [Code review](#code-review) chapter.

Full details, plus everything else cited, are in [References](#references).

::: {.tada-note}
Where this wiki adds practical detail beyond the source papers, such as a worked
README, a repository comparison table or a reviewer's script, that material is
marked as **wiki guidance** rather than presented as a finding of the papers.
:::

## Building this wiki {.unnumbered}

```bash
Rscript render.R
```

The rendered site is written to `docs/`. See [Contribute](#contribute) for the
file layout, the page template, and how to add a chapter.
